utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, Professor Bringa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Would you please stand and make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Professor Bringa, could you, first of all, give us a few details, your name, your date of birth, your place of residence, and your present occupation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Tone Bringa. My date of birth, 28/12/1960. My current address is Washington, D.C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You know that you have been called by the Court as an expert witness, and actually, we do have your book, a photocopy -- I don't know whether this was allowed by the copyright -- of your book, "Being Muslim the Bosnian Way," being published in 1995; therefore, we are already familiar with your research work, at least as it was culminated into your book of 1995. Since you are an expert witness called by the Court, we intend to proceed as follows: We will ask a few questions, general questions, to you, mainly based on your book. Then the Prosecution will examine you, or cross-examine you, and at the end, the various Defence counsel will also cross-examine you. We may, at the end of the various stages of examination, we may end up asking other questions of you. Let me, first of all, ask you to briefly recall how you carried out this research work in Dolina -- I know it is a fictitious name -- in this Muslim village. Just very briefly. You don't need to summarise the whole book, of course, just a few indications of when you went there, how you carried out this research work, and maybe the main conclusions to the extent that they're relevant to our trial. You know that we are conducting trial proceedings about some events which occurred in Ahmici on the 16th of April, '93, so therefore, I wonder whether you could focus on those features of your research work which may be of some relevance to us so as to give us the background of the relations between the Catholics, as you call them, the Catholics and the Muslims. Afterwards, we will ask you specific questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina, then part of the Yugoslav Federation, in June of 1997. I spent some weeks in Sarajevo, at the ethnographic museum there. I was looking for an appropriate rural community where I could conduct my field research, and I was interested in primarily the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as European Muslims, and to look into their customs and how they related to other groups in the area. I was interested in the relationship between the Muslims and the Christians, either the Catholics or the Orthodox Serbs. As it were, I ended up in Central Bosnia where the ethnographic museum had contacts and this particular village, which at the time consisted of a population of -- now, I haven't got the statistics with me so the number is probably not entirely accurate, but it's about 600, and two-thirds were Muslims and the rest were Catholic Bosnians or Croats, Croatian Bosnians. I stayed there for about 15 months, and I was living with a Muslim family to get an insight into everyday life and their concerns and their rituals. I followed their rituals. I observed their lives, I also participated in their lives, and that participation also consisted of socialising with the Croats in the village, going coffee-visiting -- actually, I was participating in every aspect of life in the village. Before the war, the relationship between the Muslims and the Croats was good. They did share aspects of their lives, but they also had separate lives, particularly concerning the aspect of their religious practices. The Catholics went to church and celebrated their holidays; the Muslims went to the mosque and celebrated their holidays, which separated them. But there were other aspects of life which integrated them, and particularly on an everyday basis: They cooperated about the runnings of the village, they had visited each other at life-cycle events, and they took an interest in each other's lives. Some families were more friendly with each other than others. Some neighbours, whether they were Muslim or Croat, were more friendly, and others got along -- didn't get along that well. It was like, I would say, any rural community that we know, any neighbourhood where some neighbours got along very well, and this was irrespective of whether they were Croats or Muslims or Bosniaks. It had to do with personalities, it had to do -- sometimes there were fights about borders, you know, with properties, like you have in many rural communities. There were misunderstandings, there were some quarrels, but these things then did not cut across -- it didn't cut across or it wasn't -- did not have to do with the ethnic community they belonged to. There were Croats and Muslims who were very good friends, and some Croats who were neighbours and didn't get along well and some Muslims who were neighbours that didn't get along well. My point is that, at that point, if there were conflicts in the village, it was not interpreted in terms of ethnicity, it was interpreted in other terms. But, having said that, since people did not -- okay. Let me start again. There was a potential for it, and I believe that a very important aspect of this is that kinship is very important. The Muslims and the Croats did not intermarry. So in a conflict, which could be anything from a quarrel about sheep that run into your property, these kinds of conflicts, relatives would often have strong loyalties to each other and they would stand up for each other. So you would have conflicts where people who were related sided with each other against the person that they were then in conflict with. Since Muslims and Croats didn't intermarry, you would often have -- you could have -- let me rephrase -- the potential was there for having two groups opposite each other siding with each other because of kinship ties, but they coincided with ethnic ties or ethnic identification. That is the point I want to stress: The primary loyalty was kinship at that time. As we know, ethnicity and nationalism and national rhetoric, nationalist rhetoric, often uses the idiom of kinship to have people feel like one group, to create a strong cohesion between a group, the idiom of kinship is used. You talk about it in terms of, you know, the fatherland or the motherland; you invoke these sort of strong loyalties that lie in kinship. Now, I have been talking about how it was before the war. I was saying that people there got along well irrespective of whether they were Croats or Muslims, that there were differences between people. They were very aware of these differences that had to do with, primarily, religious beliefs and religious practices, but they relished in these differences, if I may say. They were proud of them. They said, "This is Bosnia. This is how we live in Bosnia." This was truth for both the Croats in the community and the Muslims. "This is what is Bosnia. There are three different groups and we have different religions." But that wasn't -- it didn't cause communities to feel -- that wasn't -- it didn't cause animosity. They were tolerant of their differences. Now, there were some, as I said, and to sum up, some families were more friendly than others across the ethnic boundaries and others were less, and this had to do with family history, with personalities, with who was their neighbour. Now, the other thing that I have to say is that being neighbours is a very important thing in rural -- not only rural but also urban Bosnia, and the explanation I was given for that, that their first neighbour, their next-door neighbours are important, was that they said, "You know, if we are ill, if we need something, if we need help, sometimes our relatives don't live next door anymore." They used to, maybe 20, 30 years ago, there were always -- relatives used to live next door to each other and share a neighbourhood. So they said that, "Our first neighbour is the most important person because he's the nearest person." So they were careful to treat the first neighbour well. But, of course, again there were exceptions when you had a quarrel, where they didn't get along, like in so many communities. For me, this was nothing particular or nothing -- there was no -- I could not see any potential for conflict any more there than I could anywhere else that I've been. So something had to change and, to me, from what I observed and what I saw while I was there, I was there in '87/'88, I was there in 1990, in '93, '95, and '97, was that people changed gradually. As Yugoslavia disintegrated, as nationalist politics, nationalist ideologies took over the scene, people changed their perceptions of who their neighbours were. They changed identification. This is what and how do you explain, "How did they change it?" It didn't, to me, from what I saw, didn't come from within. It wasn't a change that suddenly came from within when -- what can you say -- when the communist state dissolved, it was something that was, for me, from what I saw, very clearly mobilised from outside. This was expressed again and again by people locally in how they talked about war. They would repeatedly say, you know, "We here get along. We get along." This was true for the Croats and Muslims. "What we're afraid of is people from the outside, that they come here and that they provoke things." To me, that was an expression of -- also, they would say, "This is something more powerful than us, what is going on now." Remember, this village where I was, near Kiseljak, was one of the last villages to be engulfed in the war, so they had been watching what was going on around them for a long time. First Eastern Bosnia and Northern Bosnia with the Bosnian Serb army, and then north with the clashes between the HVO and the Bosnian army. So they saw it moving closer and closer. At the same time, they were listening to propaganda on the news, and they heard about case of terror, of massacres, and they were scared. Now, I can talk a lot about how fear was whipped up and, to me, this is the key to an understanding of how ordinary people ended up behaving, and how -- let me say, as an anthropologist, I've been particularly concerned about observing people locally, observing and trying to learn about their concerns. I'm concerned with local processes but also concerned about how the larger events in -- the larger society, how politics, large-scale politics influence people locally and how it affects the dynamics between people locally, and this is what I've been observing over a period of ten years. I can say more about that if you like. I'm not sure if you want to ask some more specific questions, so whether you want me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I, for one, would like -- maybe my colleagues will ask you questions about this particular problem you have just been discussing. I, for one, would like to ask you two or three specific questions. One relates to the importance of the household in Bosnian villages, and I'm referring to page 86 and 150 of your book. I was struck by a passage in your book where you say as follows, and I will read it out: "When they lose their house, when they lose all they have worked for in the past and much of what they would have lived for in the future, and particularly" -- No. Sorry. I read -- "When they lose their house, they lose all they have worked for in the past and much of what they would have lived for in the future. Particularly for the man as father, and the house he managed to build symbolised his social worth. It was the proof of his hard work and commitment to his family and their future well-being." Then you say: "But the house of Kuca also represented the moral unity of the household and the moral quality of its members. While men were builders of the house, women were the guardians of its moral values." You have some more about the household on page 150. Now, could you elaborate on the importance of the household for families in Bosnia-Herzegovina, particularly in small villages? As you say in your book, the household is a symbol of moral values and also psychological attachments.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the house may have been particularly important during communist times because there were aspects of your religious life, of your ritual life that you could not express in public. So the arena or the place where you could express your religious beliefs, perform your religious rituals was the house, the household, the home. That was one aspect of it, because if you held a position, a higher position in Yugoslav society, you had to be a member of the Communist Party, and as a member of the Communist Party you could not express your religious beliefs in public. You could not attend public religious rituals. That was an important part of it. That was true for all the ethnic groups. But it was also where children grew up, where they learned about their -- no. They learned values, they learned about who they were through attending rituals. There again, some of the things they learned at home may have been in opposition to what they learned in school. Again, it had to do with religious beliefs and religious practices. Now, I'm not saying that these religious practices and beliefs were central in every home, because there were some homes where this was not so important, but in the rural communities particularly, there was a much more traditional approach towards religion. It was part of their whole set of customs and traditions and it wasn't something you made a conscious choice about, it was something you were born into. Now, the house was also where people -- particularly before the war and also during the war, of course, many people who lived in rural communities, they had jobs. They commuted to jobs, semi-skilled perhaps, factories in Sarajevo, but it wasn't enough to keep up a living. So they also had an income from the house, from the land that they had, and that was very much the women who then tilled the land and they had this extra income from the war. So this was very important. During the war, the home became, at least in the beginning, I think for both the Croatians and the Bosniaks, the Bosniaks more throughout the war because they had not so strong logistics support, that the home, the house became logistics support. By that I mean they went home to get fed and have their clothes cleaned and all that. That was part of the house. I'm not sure I've answered your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, no. Well, from reading your book, I got the impression that according to your research, actually, the house has tremendous importance, psychological and emotional importance for the people living in small villages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: More than as a place where you live and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: -- where you sleep, but it's also a sort of place that which is a seat of friendship, of links with other people, where you talk to other people and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I understand what you're getting at. It was -- as I say in the book as well, they spent years and years of their lives and sometimes their whole lives saving money, working very hard to build this house. They would build them in phases. They would save up money and they would be able to build the first floor. They would work very, very hard, save up more money. They didn't take up credit. They paid for it themselves and they built it themselves when they could buy some more material. So they put their -- it was also -- they would have maybe an extra floor that they'd then extend to when their children grew up. So it was an investment not only for themselves but also for the next generation. They were proud of their house. There were some people who went on migration, they went to work abroad, and they come back and build bigger houses. This was the place, particularly in winter, which can be long and cold, where people socialised. They'd meet in each other's houses. There would be Croatians visiting Muslims, Muslims visiting Croats. They sit there, they would drink coffee throughout the long nights, and they would chat about events in the village. So it was a very important place for socialising, and it was where also hospitality comes into it. Hospitality is a very important concept in Bosnia. When you have guests, you want to offer them the best. That's a way of conveying your social standing, by being able to offer the best to guests when they enter your house. You would take off your shoes when you enter a house, which is also a sign that you are now entering this distinction between the outside and the inside. This is also true for both groups. So the house is very much part of your -- the house you managed to build throughout your lifetime, when that's destroyed it's not only a physical thing that's destroyed, but it feels -- it's an attack on your whole being because you put so much into it. You put work into it but it's also what, in away, is what represents you for others. It's what tells others, to an extent, who you are, what you are, what you have achieved. That you have a nice clean home was very important. This was also true for both groups, that you were tidy, that you kept it nice. If they weren't rich and didn't have so much, they always put a lot of work into it. So it is a very important destruction, the destruction of the house. When people lost their house and it was destroyed, it was overwhelming because they couldn't see how they would find the energy to rebuild it. It was about also, of course, rebuilding their lives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Two minor questions, one about the importance of livestock. We heard a lot of evidence about the, say, cows, pigs, and so on, and I realised how much people were attached to the livestock, the animals. Is this an importance only placed on the economic value of the livestock because you get money, because you get meat, or milk, or does it go beyond the economic value of the animals? Based on your research, do you feel it's just a question of economic value?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Primarily, yes, but, again, it can take on a symbolic value, and that -- if we are now talking about Croats and Bosniaks, Croats and Muslims, it would be in terms of what kind of animals they have. Now, the Croats, they have pigs and the Muslims do not have pigs, they have sheep, which also the Croats have, but they have then -- also they have chickens. So it takes on -- it's more not having the livestock but it's more what you eat, and that is a distinctive trait between the two groups, that the Croats eat pork while the Muslims don't. But this is something, actually, before the war, they were very respectful towards each other about this, at least from what I observed in the families that I knew, when a Muslim visited Croat households, they would be respectful of this. They would not serve them anything with pork fat. So I don't think there really is very much more to that. In this particular village, actually, there was one shepherd, he was a Croat, and he took care of the livestock, the sheep, of both the Muslims and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have two more questions, one is a minor question, but in your book, on page 39, you point out that it was easy to distinguish Catholic houses from Muslim houses because the Muslim houses were square, as is the village mosque, you say, while the Catholic houses were rectangular, except for one, as you say on page 57, there was just one house which did not fit in this sort of distinction. We heard evidence about the roof. I thought the main difference was to be found in the different shapes of the roofs, but I understand from your book, actually, that the whole house had a different shape in the case of Catholics and in the case of Muslims. Was it easy for an outsider to distinguish between a Catholic and a Muslim house just because of the different shape of the house, one was square, one was rectangular -- some were rectangular --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are a few things. Well, of course, the roof affects the shape of the building. Now, I think what I described on that page is the upper part of the village, the old part. It's a village that stretches out, so in the new part of the village, there were many more houses that were the same. There were newer houses, built often by younger people and people who had earned money abroad, and they, you could not distinguish between the Croat and the Bosniak houses. In the upper part, the old part, this is true, there was only one, and the Croat houses often have a cross carved in up underneath the roof. Now, for an outsider, again, if they know about these differences, they could tell. Now, I'm not sure -- I think it's very specific to Bosnia and particularly Central Bosnia, and I don't know whether they would know about it. That, I have no idea about. But also, of course, every village would have houses that were not distinct in this way. The newer houses would not be distinct; they'd look more -- they would sort of be, I would say, probably inspired by architecture in Austria or something like that, I don't know. So, again, some houses could be, if you knew about these distinctions, and other houses couldn't. You would need to know who lived there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: As a result, somebody coming from outside, say from a different area, region, or a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it would not be easy to immediately identify Catholic or Croat houses on the one side and Muslim houses on the other side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe not. If they did not know about this distinction or if houses were -- there were many houses that were the same, were newer structures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, my last question in a way is linked up to what you said at the outset when you spoke about the potential for conflict. I am reading in particular page 67 and the following pages where you speak of the shared values. I was wondering whether, actually, already in 1988, when you carried out most of your research work in a Bosnian village, you identified some seeds of hatred, of ethnic or religious hatred. Actually, it amounts to -- it boils down to asking you to elaborate on what you said before when you spoke about the potential for conflict. Yes. You call it "potential for conflict." I would term it "seeds of ethnic or religious tension or friction or hatred."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I already said, as in any community, close-knit community, there are potential for conflicts, which are often based in quarrels about property, differences which have to do with different personalities and so on. But, of course, the fact that Bosniaks and Croats distinguished themselves by religion means that there is a great symbolic potential -- let me rephrase. There are strong symbols to play on for somebody who would like to play out the differences between people, and I believe that it is really, again, it is up to -- it is not something that can just develop from the inside, there has to be something else that puts this in motion, and it depends, you know, you can -- as somebody who governs an area, who is in a position of power, they can stress the potential for harmony, for living together, because that was just as strong, if not even stronger, they can stress what these people have in common, what they shared; but you can also stress what's different and what separates these people, but you can stress it in such a way that it becomes a negative, it becomes a threat. Yes, there were instances in the village, as I said, but then often it wasn't interpreted in terms of ethnicity. Now, what was happening? There has been a lot of talk about ethnic hatreds of Bosnia and that they were present and they were kept in check by Titoism. I see it differently. I did not see ethnic hatreds. What I saw was an escalating fear, I saw increasing fear, and fear that eventually, through violence, through terror, through harassment, turned into hatred. Something had to be done to people. They had to change the way they perceived the other. Now, I can give you an example. While war was raging -- this was in January 1993 -- while war was raging around this area, people were still, although slightly started to -- communities started to separate because the men, the Croat men, participated in one army and the Bosniak men participated in a different army and they were clashing for the north, but they were still trying to keep up relations, particularly the women who weren't separated in armies. But I would then hear, in this particular instance, I would hear a young -- this was an incident, it just happened to be a young Croat who said -- who talked about the Muslims in very general terms. They were rather racist, you know. He was using these denigrating terms for Muslims and talking about, in very general terms, that they were out to get them, that -- well, things that I recognised from some of the propaganda that was sent over the media, the Croatian-controlled media. Now, he was saying -- and that suddenly switched because he started talking about his next-door neighbour, who was a Muslim, and he said, "Well, he's very -- he's okay. He's very nice." And he tried to talk about him in very individual -- you know, in terms of personality traits and that he liked him and that he trusted him and that he had nothing to do with this other group, that was a very general term, "out there," the Muslims "out there." Now, at one point, this is a process whereby -- then this young man that I'm using as an example, he could be any young man, starts associating this next-door neighbour that he knew well, that he grew up with, with that larger group of Muslims who are out to get them or threaten them or ... And then, at that point, when that happens, he distances himself from his neighbour and his neighbour becomes just "they," "the enemy," he loses all his personal traits, he becomes an individual identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I wanted to find out about the families. In the Muslim families, was there any distinction in terms of, I would say, human value between sons and daughters? Would their family prefer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say there was any distinction in human value, but they would just -- in this rural community, which was quite traditional, they were brought up to take care of different aspects of life. They were given different roles, they were even given different tasks. Having said that -- no, there wasn't a difference, but it was important often to have a son because the son is what continues the line. It is -- what should we say? -- call it a patrilineal society where the name is carried from father to son.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So would you say that the birth of a son would be celebrated more than the birth of a daughter, or if a family had sons only, they would be much happier than those who had only daughters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I really -- I can't -- I'm going through my mind to see whether there were any such cases. It was a great event when a baby was born. I can say it was important to have a son, but I can't speak for these families that then only had daughters. I would assume they were happy with the daughters, that they didn't treat -- you know, express anything that would have me say that they were not happy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm asking this question because the evidence we have received was that the killings were to eliminate the male line, for instance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, if this is -- this is what you -- I would again say that it was important because it continued the family, but I can't talk about whether people were disappointed or unhappy if they only had daughters, but it was important to be able to continue the line. And also men, of course, eventually became soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I think it is now for the Prosecution to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Terrier:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Franck Terrier, I am one of the representatives for the Prosecution in this trial, and I am going to ask you in French a few questions further to your testimony and after I have read your book and learned about the film in which you participated which was broadcast by the BBC. You lived in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1986 and '87 for 15 months. Could you clarify what the period was when you went back to that village that we will call Dolina?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: Yes. I went back first in 1990, which is just prior to the elections, it was in the middle of the election campaign, and I went back then again in 1993. I went back in January of 1993. I spent three weeks there in January, and I believe the dates were January the 22nd to February the 14th. Then we left on the 14th. We then learnt from the U.N. headquarters that the village had been attacked, so we went back, and this was in April, we went back April 29th, and I was there until May the 3rd. This is in 1993. Then I went back in '95 and, as I said, in '97.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The film broadcast by the BBC, which is called "We Were All Neighbours," therefore was filmed in January and February and then in April and May of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. Your Honour, shall we show this film or -- can I assume that everybody has seen it and simply refer to it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Is it a very long film? We didn't see it, we Judges. It would be interesting to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, I think it would be. It is a film which runs for about 50 minutes. It is the film that was made for the BBC essentially by the witness and in the village that we are speaking about in the book, at the beginning of 1993, and then after the events of April, toward the end of April and May 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Did you give the cassette to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I believe I did, yes. I think that we gave it at the same time as we gave the copy of the book; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecutor probably got confused. He did give us a copy of the book, to the representatives of the Defence; however, we never received a copy of the film, so we cannot say anything about it. If questions are going to be put in relation to the film, we would like to see it too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it would be worth seeing. All right. We are going to see the film. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: There is no translation, I understand, for Defence counsel, Bosnian or Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have a transcript in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Perhaps the interpreters could help us out with that? Let me turn to the interpreters. Could you interpret from English into Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are saying that they can try but that they can't guarantee the exactness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The Prosecutor doesn't have a transcript. Well, let's try to have some interpretation. It won't be perfect, but we can have some. All right. We can start from the beginning. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Before we take a break, may I ask the Prosecutor whether they're going to tender the document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would add that when we spoke about Tone Bringa's book, I was also speaking about the film. Both of them are absolutely unassociable (sic). The same people that we see in the film are those that are spoken about in the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection from the Defence counsel? No objection. So it is admitted into evidence and we will adjourn now for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If you allow me, I would like to give some information briefly to the Tribunal. On the 6th of October, 1998, in this courtroom we spoke about the suitability or appropriateness of giving to the Tribunal the book, "Being Muslim the Bosnian Way" and the film "We Are All Neighbours." The court decided that we should present the film and the book and to disclose them both to the Defence. We assert that we did that on the 12th of October, 1998, and on the 15th of October, 1998 there was a new discussion, a further discussion, I'm referring to the transcript, that was on the 12th, in which I say that I disclose those documents that are pending before the court and which were given to the Defence in accordance with the instructions of the Trial Chamber. These are the instructions that I can give you after having checked on this during the break, but I hope this will not be the source of any type incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, just a brief clarification. It is correct what my colleague from the Prosecution has said. However, we initially received only a summarised version of it, and then we requested to be given the whole version, which we received as a photocopy, and it was a single set. That is all. The Defence has no reason to deny that it had received this tape, but we never received the book and this is what I submit to you. After the Prosecution is finished with their examination, we can see whether this was relevant for our examination. Again, I would like to underscore that we never received the cassette but we do not want to raise any problems over it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I find it very strange. I mean, you hand over both the book and the videotape to the Defence, and they -- you never got the videotape. But you did receive the book, I mean, the photocopy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Later. Only the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We only received the book, no videotape or a transcript of this videotape. But again, let me emphasise: The Defence is not going to raise that as an objection, as a problem. Again, I don't want to repeat myself, but we will just wait out to see what the Prosecution is going to make of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Pavkovic. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Bringa, the individuals we saw in the cassette are those that you described -- whose lives you described in your book; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them. Some of the people who appear are in the book. Sorry, let me rephrase that. Some of the people who appear in the book are also in the film.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would appear that in April of 1993, the village which we call Dolina was attacked by the HVO. In your book, I believe it's page 16 of the preface, you state that the attack had been prepared by foreigners from outside the village but that some Croats who lived in the village had participated in that preparation. Could you tell us what your source is for stating that?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: Could I look up -- could I see that page just so that I'm sure I get it straight, please? Okay. I don't know quite where to start because this was obviously a process that went on for some time. It was clear that -- well, I can give you one example that may illustrate what you're asking me. When we first arrived in the village in January, the Muslims and the Croats in the village had held common patrols in the upper part of the village, which is where the settlement was most dense and the houses of Croats and Muslims were closest to each other. So they went in groups of two, two Croats and two Muslims, to guard their houses, because they still have this opinion that they could protect themselves from outsiders and it would be an attack which would be waged by outsiders. Now, during our stay there, these common patrols, they discontinued. I asked -- there was one particular Muslim in the village who was very -- who was very central in organising these patrols, and when I asked him why they did not hold common patrols any more, he said that his Croat neighbours had got orders to discontinue them. Now, did I ask the Croats who went in the patrols? No, I did not. This is maybe something you will return to, but we were not allowed to film Croat men in uniform in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay in May of 1993, did you have any conversations with representatives of UNPROFOR? In the film we see that you could go back to Dolina with the assistance of a vehicle from UNPROFOR. Did the soldiers give you any information about what had happened in Dolina?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: Yes. When we left in February, we knew that there was a campaign going on in the area, and we also knew that the area was under the control of the HVO and that reading, listening to the media, reading newspapers, and listening to how local Croats were talking about it, we knew this was an area they considered theirs, which I'm sure you've been talking about before, meaning this would be part of their territory that they would control under the peace plan, particularly the Vance-Owen Plan. In Bosnia and the former Yugoslavia, because it lacked the democratic tradition, when one side was in control that meant total control. Power sharing was not a known phenomena, except -- and also representation in political, full-out wars on the basis of ethnicity. Now, it was an area which was considered by the Croatian local government and the HVO as a Croat area. We then knew this and we kept in touch. The only way to keep in touch -- we were trying to find out what was happening. We called the UNPROFOR headquarters in Kiseljak, and they told us that there had been fighting and that village had been attacked, but they didn't know much more than that. They hadn't been there yet to see. So we made a decision -- we were discussing what to do. We made a decision to go back and try and find out what had happened. We left in two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to go back to the idea of neighbourliness that you mentioned in the book, particularly on page 65 and on the following pages. You say, if I've understood you correctly, you state that between the two communities, that is, the Muslim and the Croat community, over the years and perhaps even over scores of years, social relationships that were very specific had developed, relationships that were almost ritualised, whose object was to provide security for everybody in the village. Did I understand what you said in the book correctly in respect of the relationship between neighbours?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: If you could just specify what you mean by "security."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm merely referring to the fact that each of the members in the community that found themselves living as neighbours in the village, wanted to avoid any source of conflict.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have the feeling that these neighbourly relationships were able to operate because in some way, and specifically during the period before the elections of November 1990, the state authorities, that is, the Federal state authorities, guaranteed them, and that when that authority disappeared, the neighbourly relationships became very fragile and could no longer ensure that the various inhabitants of the various communities would be able to live in safety.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: I don't know what you have in mind particularly. I don't know which way the Federal authorities would secure neighbourliness since this is something that grows out of the situation on an individual basis, and it's nothing -- a state can't control people's emotions and their everyday life to a certain extent. So I disagree with that. I do not believe it was the Federal authorities that guaranteed that people -- neighbourliness, that people went along, that they visited each other for coffee, that they shared in each other's life-cycle events, that they took a real interest in each other and that they cared for each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your book, you state that as regards the relationship between the neighbours, the members of each of the communities had the very strong feeling of belonging to a community which was not the other one. The Muslims know that they were not Croats and the Croats know that they are -- that they're Croats and not Muslims. In particular, you mentioned the notion of interethnic marriages. You state that those marriages were not looked upon with a favourable eye or at least were not really approved of by the inhabitants. In the village of Dolina, were there any interethnic marriages; that is, one of the two spouses would be a member of a different community or both would be?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: Yes. There were two to my knowledge. There were two between a Muslim man and a Serb woman. There were one that -- there were two that I knew of, but they moved out of the village, between a Croat man and a Muslim woman, but they'd moved out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Ms. Bringa, what it was in the village's daily life, that is, that village of Dolina, what distinguished one community from the other in daily life? Was it the way people dressed, the way people ate, the cultural customs, things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: There were a set of things and some these things that are mentioned have changed over time, like the dress. Older Muslim women would wear dimija, they're baggy trousers, and they wear a headscarf. Actually, there was an old Croat woman in the village who was also wearing dimija and a headscarf. Several of them, as you saw, were wearing headscarves. So this was actually common, that 20, 30 years ago all women would wear dimija, although, the Catholic women would wear black. So they were distinguished by colour. For the younger generation, there were not any differences, any concrete differences. There were perceptions about it some ways, that some of the more modern, fashionable girls would consider -- Muslim girls, particularly from further up the village, I think it was rather a class thing than it was ethnic thing, but they didn't dress as modern. But this is more to do with education, with the fact that you go to urban areas and such influences. There were differences, as I mentioned before, in what they ate. Croat Catholics would cook in pork fat, which gave a particular smell when you cooked, and the Muslims would cook in oil, which would give a different smell. They would recognise these smells in each other's houses, and there would be -- you know, pork was a difference. Otherwise, of course, religion and the holidays. The Croats, they celebrated, Christmas, Christian Christmas, and Easter, and other Christian holidays. The Muslims celebrated the Islamic holidays. The interesting thing was that there was exchange during these times. There was a tradition during Easter, for instance, that the Catholic children, Catholic Croat children, they would paint eggs and come and give them to Muslim children. At the Muslim holiday of Bajram, they would invite their Croat neighbours for the cakes and sharing the sweet cakes with them. So they visited each other, although, when it was -- when the religious ritual took place in the mosque, in the church, of course, obviously they were separate. But they went to the same schools. They worked in the same factories. They shopped in the same shops. They did the same things. They were sharing in the local council which took care of village affairs. There was one Croat, one Muslim. They cared for the community together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that you say in your book that during that period before the war, the feelings of difference changed into something else, something of foreignness, that the other person became the enemy. I don't have the exact reference in my mind, but I think you say that someplace. In your opinion, how can one explain this change, this sudden change from the other, the foreigner, into the enemy, during the months and weeks that preceded the time in question?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: I think that the woman we saw in the film, Slavka, explains it very well, and although it appeared to the individuals that finally changed their perception as something sudden, it suddenly happened, they had been under pressure for some time. Now, what she says, she says, "It's difficult to understand," and she talks how the war moves closer, and that they always shared in things and that they lived together, and as long as it was out there and it didn't affect them personally, the war, the clashes between the HVO and the Bosnian army, which involved men and also civilians, as you know, so long as it was out there and nobody in the village was affected, they could distance themselves from it and say, "It's a war between two units," you know, and, "We're not -- it's not concerning us. We will manage to stay in peace. Then when it moves closer, like if somebody near to you, somebody you know, is hurt, then it changes. But also, what she says is that, "I don't understand it." You know, "I changed my perceptions in one day," is how she says this. It doesn't mean one day, but it's to express her suddenness. But she says -- which wasn't translated in the film because some things -- we couldn't translate everything, you know, with reading the subtext, she says that that thing was created. She said, "Stvaranje. That was created," and she does like this (witness demonstrating). This is -- a Muslim woman told me the same thing. She said, "It's something bigger than us." What was this bigger than them? Well, it was propaganda constantly in the media. The radio station at the time was run from -- which the Croats listened to was run from Grude in Herzegovina, and it constantly was repeating these things, that the Muslims were wanting to create a state where there was no place for the Croats, where they may be massacred, killed. They would exclude them and they would talk about the Muslims in that degenerating way. They would use words that were -- I could say -- call them racist, meaning that they described them in a very -- as a less -- being of less value. They would constantly talk about what the enemy -- they would use terms, the language would be "enemy," "of the enemy," and what they were up to and what they would do to the Croats. Also, at the same time, of course, playing on Croatian national symbols, religious symbols, the flag, as we saw. The idea then also that things happened. There were violent incidents. There were massacres. You don't necessarily need a massacre by the opposite group to give the message that you're in danger. It can just as well be a massacre that your own group have committed against the other, because it would give the message that, you know, "As long as you're one of us, you're okay. We'll protect you ." But if you're not, you're in danger. You'll be, you known, defined as the enemy. This escalation of fear, that people don't have anything to hold onto, anything secure, their daily lives are disrupted. The things that were certain points that they could hold onto in life aren't there any more; they're disoriented. What do people do? This is very general. This is a process that happens in similar situations everywhere. They withdraw into secure groups where loyalty is not a question because you are born into the group; your membership is not questioned, you don't have to qualify. It is very easy. This is the nation, it is the ethnic group, the kinship group, which has this thing in common, its nation is spoken about in terms of blood ties. So you're born into it. This is secure. You withdraw more and more and more and the enemy is out there, and as soon as you stop socialising with the representatives of this so-called "other group," you have no way of checking reality, you have no way of checking whether all this propaganda that you are absorbing, you have no way of checking it against reality. Who are these people? So you are building up an enemy picture. You want to protect yourself and, in the end, the only protection is, you feel, with your own group, that group that you're defined as a member of. I don't know if that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you've answered my question. But your answer gives rise to another question: Are you familiar with another period of history, for example, the history of Europe or the history of another continent, where propaganda like that that you described did not extend over a long time, only a few months? Do you know of other examples when propaganda would cause such serious and such intense problems? By that I mean, I am thinking about different episodes from history where propaganda transformed neighbours or communities into enemies but the propaganda went on over a much greater amount of time, was much more intense than the propaganda you were referring to a little while ago, that is, Busovaca Television or Kiseljak Television. Wasn't there something very specific in this case which was unprecedented and which, in the end, is not something that one can explain?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: No, I actually believe that the explanation is quite simple, and I do think that this was not something that happened in Bosnia because the Bosnians are particularly prone to it, but in those sort of circumstances that I was in, you have to have a particular mixture of circumstances when this becomes possible, that people change their perceptions, they change their idea of identity, and they are willing to go out and, you know, kill people of the opposite group. This is a process where -- well, it is a long story, but it has to do with the dissolution of Yugoslavia, it has to do with the economic situation, it has to do particularly about the kind of leadership that were voted into power and what sort of symbols they were using, what sort of rhetoric they were using to mobilise people to support them. Now, has it happened other times in history? Yes, I believe it has. I believe it is a well-known recipe, a well-known cocktail of nationalist propaganda, of racist propaganda, where the people who believe in the superiority of their own group are willing to also expel that group that may not go along with their plans, and I don't want to mention a particular incident but I can only guess that you have had similar processes in Rwanda, for instance, you have had similar processes in Europe during the Second World War when a nationalist ideology forced people into homogeneous groups where they were willing to commit atrocities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you feel in 1987, 1988, and then in 1993, that the members of the Croatian community that you were able to meet with made references to the history of their country and their community? In their daily life, was this an important aspect?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: It was not mentioned before the war. The only few references I had then were humorous ones about -- there was the priest in the area, a Catholic priest, and a Muslim family had the same surname, so they made humorous jokes about, you know, how this came about and that probably the brother of his great-grandfather or something had turned to Islam some hundred years ago. That was the only reference then because there was no history of conflict between the Croats and the Muslims in this area. But what I did -- yes, I did in 1993 when I was back, and to me it sounded like not something that they had actually suddenly realised but something that they had either read or heard somewhere. There were references to, for instance, that all the land there was really Croatian land, it should be owned by the Croats because the Muslims took it away from them during the Ottoman times and it originally had been their land. That was one comment that was made. Beyond that, yes, that this part, that Bosnia was really Croatia, had been a part of Croatia, but there wasn't that much actual reference to history as you would see on the Bosnian Serb side, I believe because there was actually -- there had been -- the last contention about history.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When one looks at the videotape, one has the feeling that the Muslims who expressed themselves found themselves on the defensive, that was in January and February of 1993, and that the members of the Croatian community had more assurances and felt more sure themselves and had a greater will to conquer people, the idea of a defensive Muslim community and a conquering type of Croatian community makes me wonder whether what you saw corresponds with what we saw in the film.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your last comment, but I will comment on the first part of it. Yes, there was definitely the idea on the Croatian side that this now was theirs and that they were in control. One way -- I can give you several examples. For instance, the local kindergarten where they decided -- this was before -- I guess in '92, when they decided to celebrate, for the children, Christmas, and one of the employees, who I think was a Serb woman, said, "What about, you know, Muslim Bajram and Orthodox Christmas?" And she said, "Well, you know" -- this was the person in charge there -- "Those who want to celebrate Bajram, they can move to Visoko, and those who want to celebrate Orthodox Christmas can move to, I don't know, Foca, or somewhere." So there was an idea that this was now Croatian territory, and they also said, you know, that the Muslims now are -- you know, they're like in the bottom of a fildjan -- a fildjan is a small coffee cup without handles -- and they can't go anywhere, they can't go up, they can't go down, you know, to the sides, so what are they going to do with this little fildjan, which was a way of talking about what was left of the Bosnia that the Sarajevo government was controlling? There were lots of comments like that, but there was definitely -- they were in control, you saw on the film and that was the case, it was HVO that controlled the area, it was HVO we had to ask permission from for filming, it was -- we had to go through HVO checkpoints to get into Kiseljak. Muslims were scared of going in, and if they did, you saw they went by bus or walked because if they went by car, the car was taken away from them. This happened. And if Muslim men went in, they were -- Muslim men of fighting age, that is, they were taken into the police station for interrogation. So there was increasing pressure. The Muslim aid organisation that delivered food and aid to the Muslims, the Merhamet, was closed down. The person who led it was arrested. So there was some increasing intensity, you know, and the pressure on the Muslims increased and they were getting increasingly worried, and a parallel thing did not happen to the Croatian community in this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a final question, Ms. Bringa. It has to do with religious practices and the mosque. In your book you say that the Dolina mosque was in the middle of the village. In any case, in the neighbourhood, the Muslim neighbourhood, in that village, whereas the Catholic church was on the outside. Did each community's religious practices have so much importance for the community and were those practices tolerated by the other community? Was tolerance something which was real when you were in the village or was there a change in that respect?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: When I was there at the end of the '80s, yes, I mean, this was the way it always had been as long as these people could remember and also their parents before them, that there had been a mosque in the village where the Muslims went and they knew, you know, the Croat -- and there was a church that actually was quite derelict in the early '80s but had been rebuilt which was on the outside of the village, it was in a different part of this opstina, this commune. They had always observed each other -- I mean, they knew about each other's holidays. They sometimes got it slightly wrong. And this was the way it had always been. And they would ask about each other's holiday a bit. And the Muslims would go to the mosque and they would have their -- and funerals, for instance, was an interesting thing because Muslims would attend -- if a Croat in the village that they had been friendly with, if he had Muslim friends, they would attend the funeral and vice versa, and they were made -- if there was, say -- now, according to Islam, women are not allowed to attend at the ceremony by the graveyard, they can stay in the house, but they accommodated, if there was a woman who was Christian who wanted to attend because she knew the deceased, they would let her attend and do it her way, lay flowers on the grave or do it her way to express her sorrow or her respects in her way. So this was -- it's always been there and it wasn't something that suddenly had come from the outside and suddenly people had to try and adapt to this presence of this group with different practices or a different religion, this was -- the whole dynamic of the community was like that. Did it change? Well, I'm not sure what you mean. Of course, because religion was the main distinguishing factor, the aspects of religion fed into the propaganda by using negative terms about religion by, maybe in some instances, ridiculing it, but then -- and obviously the Muslim religious buildings were destroyed. They weren't destroyed -- the mosque was destroyed and another religious building, which is a holy grave, was destroyed, not in the attack in April but they went back in July. I was told it happened in July. It wasn't destroyed in May. And so -- but also there was the religious leadership -- I mean, this is very individual, but I know the priest in this particular area, he talked about peace and cohabiting in peace for a long time, but there were others who didn't so it's ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your book I believe you said, at the end of 1993, there was not a single Muslim in the village of Dolina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: Sorry. Which date was it you mentioned in ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of 1993, December 1993.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: December 1993. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what has happened to them since or what has happened since? Did the Muslims come back?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: Yes, I know what has happened since. They have lived as internally displaced. Some people were killed. Some were killed while they were kept in a neighbouring village in a couple of houses for a long time and were not allowed to go anywhere. Some died then. They lived as internally displaced people in other parts of the region where the Sarajevo government was in control, where the Bosnian army was in control, and they are, actually, now, as we speak, moving back, and I've spoken to them about it and they say that their neighbours who are still there are treating them okay in the village, the people in the village I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your testimony, Ms. Bringa. Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Pavkovic, can you tell us who is going to cross-examine this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Defence attorneys would like to ask for a brief five-minute break so that we could agree on a common position with regard to the video footage we saw, and then we'll take a position with regard to cross-examination as well. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So we will now take a very short break of five minutes -- do you think five minutes will be sufficient? Five. All right. A five-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Is there any problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No. There was not a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: On behalf of the Defence attorneys, I wish to inform you that we do accept this video cassette and we can move on to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: However, I will have a few questions for the witness, and then I would like to announce Mr. Par and then Mr. Pasaric.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video cassette will be 373, Prosecutor's Exhibit 373.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasaric is my co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Your co-counsel. All right. So we start with Counsel Pavkovic, then Counsel Parr, and then Counsel Pasaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Pavkovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Petar Pavkovic, attorney at law. I think it would be a good thing if you had a copy of your book with you, and I would like us to discuss the contents and I would like to ask you for a few comments, please. In the introductory part of this book, on page number 5, 5, the numeral 5, in the last sentence of the first section, you said the following -- I mean, I am going to briefly present it the way I understood your message. You were saying that it was not your intention for this research to apply to all of Bosnia and its entire population. It is only a detailed study of one link in the chain, as you put it very picturesquely, that Bosnia consists. My question is the following: Is this place that you did your research in then a representative sample of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: Yes. I do state -- I do not say it's not my intention that it should not apply to all of Bosnia but I do say that this is one strand in that weave that makes the Bosnian -- makes Bosnia. You asked me whether it applies to all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. No, it does not, because, for instance, there are parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina where there were Serbs and Muslims who live together. This, I think, although this is a particular village, and I'm very careful to say that, and particular people with their idiosyncrasies, there are some general traits that I think we could generalise to a larger community. I think -- because this is not the only place I went to. I visited other parts of Central Bosnia. We would take or leave some specifics which had to do with the composition of the village, with the history of the village, with the particular people who lived there, there are certain general traits, and I think through this microcosm, you can also come to an understanding of what was going on in a wider context, but, as I said, take or leave specific aspects of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have understood your point. So as a scholar, you cannot say that this would be ... You, as a scholar, you cannot say that this would be a sample that could be applied to the entire area; did I understand you correctly? Is it specific in many aspects?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: Well, let me try and rephrase it. I believe that this is a microcosm, and indeed I do not only describe that particular village and those particular houses but I do also talk about the larger region, and this microcosm is a mirror of -- it does give us insight into other communities that have similar compositions that are in the same geographical area, that have the same history. What I'm thinking about now particularly are communities where Croats and Muslims lived together, where Croats and Muslims shared the geographical space. And again, as I was saying, other parts of Bosnia, Eastern Bosnia, say, the history and the dynamics between people were different because there was a -- it was inhabited by Serbs and Muslims, say, others again by Serbs and Croats. So this is my reservation. There are particular, very specific things, but the fact remains that there were Croats there, there were Muslims there. The Croats are Catholics; the Muslims practised Islam. They lived within the same -- again, you know, they attended school over a larger area. They knew each other -- again, this is, you know, Bosnia, it had short distances. People know each other over a larger area. There are relatives, you know, kinship networks are spread over. They moved up, to the sides, they would move further north to the towns. In this whole area, people interacted. It wasn't as if this was an island in the whole region of Central Bosnia. People had relatives, they knew each other, they worked with people from other towns, other communities, they went to school with them. That's really my point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Lest there be any misunderstanding, lest there be any misunderstanding, when I'm quoting parts of your book to you, certain sentences, as I shall do straightaway, I would like you to understand that I'm not taking them out of context. That is not my intention. But I would simply like you to comment on them for me. Further on, on page 5 of the introduction, in the first paragraph, you say, when you're talking about your intention, you say that this book or the material that you used for it does not intend to explain the war for a simple reason, because the war was not started by villagers who were the subject of your research. Furthermore, you say that this war was orchestrated from other places where the villagers from the village where you lived were not represented and their voice could not have been heard in those places. Did I understand the gist of what you were saying? I would just like you to comment on that now because the questions that were put by the Prosecutor relate to the war. We saw it here too. But you were involved in ethnology because that is your line of work and that is what you are qualified for; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: I'm not an ethnologist, I'm an anthropologist. I know there are -- I know -- sorry, there are sort of differences, differences mainly --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: Ethnologists, they deal with only local, very local, issues, and anthropologists, they're comparative, and that is a very important aspect of our work. There are subdisciplines and we also -- as I said initially here, anthropologists are focusing in particular on local dynamics, and people locally and how they -- their concerns and social organisation, how they live their lives, but, of course, we have to look at also the larger political context because that plays down, it plays into the local communities. It is not -- they are not islands, as I said before. There is an interaction between those levels, and decisions made on a higher level have consequences for people locally. I do say it does not intend to explain the war, because -- well, part of it was mainly taking part -- no, taking place before the war, and that's what I wanted to describe. I wanted to describe how these people lived together, what sort of lives they had before the war, because during the -- in particular, a lot of the media coverage of this war, you had the impression that there had always been fighting. This is one of the things that does not intend to explain the war. But I do think that through reading about how these people lived together, how they interacted, what their concerns were, that you can gain an understanding of how things must have changed. Then the question is: How could they change and what provoked that change? I think it's a document that shows very well that it couldn't just have appeared from within. There was something else. There was the process. There was a dynamic. There was something that caused a change in this village. This is -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, I would like to apologise if I caused a misunderstanding, offended you, whatever. My last question: On page XVII, Roman numeral XVII, in the second paragraph you are talking about a problem that you encountered when you decided to write this book, and you say that this problem concerning the time that you were supposed to write about, and that this is -- that this tends -- that anthropological studies are written in the present tense, and you said that the Muslims would often confuse their tenses. They would sometimes speak in the past tense, they would sometimes speak in the present tense, and that all of it had a lack of reality. So we're talking about '93, and this was the time of the conflict and after the conflict. What is your view of this? How did they present the war to you? What is the picture of war that they painted for you in the immediate aftermath?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: Well, first on confusing the tenses. It wasn't really a lack of reality, it was the fact that something had been there. Their lives had suddenly been destroyed, disrupted. They talked about, you know, "Our houses. Where we live," but then suddenly, you know, two weeks ago they'd lived there and they'd had lives in the community, and then now they are refugees. This is in the context of them having been expelled from the village and having lost everything. Then, of course, for my presence again, which reminded them of the past of their lives. It takes time for a person. You know, it's a shock, and it takes time to realise what has happened to you. So this is the reason for them not -- you know, switching tenses. They would talk -- some moments they realised, "Yes, we have lost this all," so they would talk about the village and their life there in the past tense, but then other moments when they talked to me this was not real yet because it takes time for a person to realise when you've gone through something like that. So that was my only -- it wasn't that they were confused in such a sense that they didn't know what had happened, it was just a question of when you recounted things. But they referred to their lives, not what had happened exactly then and there during the war. The second part of your question was: How did they talk about the war to me. I wonder, could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this same paragraph that I referred to, that is to say, in the second paragraph on page XVII of your forward, you say that you discovered that the Muslims were switching from one tense to another, and that they were bringing the past and the present together in a strange way, with a lack of reality. That was the point of my question. What was your assessment of this when they were explaining these events to you? If I understood things correctly, you were talking about this lack of a sense of reality.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: Let me say again, when they are talking about the past and the present, the points where they were confusing tenses were when they were referring to their lives in the village, their houses, what has now gone. It was not to do with a past further back or had to do with the past and the present in that instance where they were attacked, it had to do solely when they talked about, you know, "Up in my house we are...," you know, and then they realised the house doesn't exist any more. It wasn't -- it was -- they were very aware of fact that they -- you know, in moments they -- yeah. Okay. We saw them very soon after this. So I'm still not quite sure what you're getting at. You want me to talk about how they talked about what had happened to them? Is that what you'd like me to talk about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: How they explained --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What am I trying to get at? I'm going to tell you straightaway. The way they portrayed events to you. Was this realistic? What was your assessment, in view of these tenses that you've been speaking about, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: Oh, yes, of course. I mean, I think people who take in witness proofs from people who have been the victims of war, of atrocities, whatever, that they can tell when there's actually been -- something you're talking about that has happened to you. This was not something they'd made up. This had happened to them. We saw what had happened in the village. They had no reason to make this up. It was so clear to me. They had left. They were in distress. They were distraught. They had no possessions with them. They were now leaving under very bad conditions, gathered in one room, you know, 20, 30 of them, and there was no reason for them to, you know, make this up. On the other hand, people can't -- I don't think they can act their emotions like that. That, coupled the fact that we'd saw and we'd been there prior to this, the attack of the village, makes the picture, I think, very clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for having answered all my questions. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Par:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good day, Madam Professor. My name is Zelimir Par, and I'm one of the Defence attorneys here, and I would appreciate it if you would answer a few questions. At the outset, I would like to ask you about the contacts that you had with these persons in the village after having filmed this programme or, rather, in which time period did you last have contact with these persons? What was the year, the month?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: I was there last time -- I visited some of the people, obviously just a few of them because they're scattered all over. I was there last in 1997.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in relation to your meetings with them, I would like to know whether in the meantime they had changed some of their views regarding their suffering and all these events. I'm interested in hearing the following: Do they still think, until the present day, as they said in the film, that there can be no life together, and do they condemn their Croat neighbours to that same extent today? Do they hold them responsible as they did in the time of their greatest suffering? To put it more specifically, are they even more critical today with regard to these events than they were before?

utterances.speaker: TONE BRINGA
utterances.text: Okay. Let me make a distinction. There were people -- local Croats in the village that -- like the one that described in the film, who did actually kill a neighbour, who participated in that kind of way, who they still condemn. But there has also been a change, yes, in the way people talk about the conflict. I believe, and I hope on both sides, whereby -- and I think this is part of the peace process that's taking place and new leadership's coming in, new leaders -- that they are talking about it as -- they're talking about not the attack of the Croats, they're talking about the attack of the HVO. So they are ascribing individual responsibility. There were also -- which, for reasons that I'm very sorry now but has to do the whole way you edit a film, which I cannot go into details here, but Croats who did, in the village -- there were Croats who participated and there were Croats who stood by. There were also Croats who protected their neighbours, and obviously they still feel very warm towards them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I should stop you precisely at this point. Specifically, I'm interested in the following: In the immediate aftermath of their suffering, when you talked to them then, did they say, at that time, that they held their Croat neighbours accountable for these crimes, so to speak, or did they give you specific names or did they make a distinction at the time? Did they say, "Such and such a neighbour did not take part?" or, "Such and such a neighbour did take part?" or did they speak in general terms, the Croats? I'm bearing in mind that you knew Croats from that village too. You knew their neighbours. You knew them personally; right?
